title: Reperfusion of established retinal capillary dropout

concept.text: The proposed innovation is restoration of durable, functional blood circulation in retinal regions after established capillary loss. The goal is a connected capillary network that carries blood through the affected tissue, supplies oxygen, and maintains the blood–retina barrier without pathological leakage or bleeding. This would extend beyond preserving surviving capillaries or suppressing abnormal vessel growth. The supplied evidence documents the unmet reperfusion goal and experimental capillary preservation, but does not demonstrate reconstruction of a chronically depleted human retinal capillary network.

A crucial distinction is whether vessels have disappeared anatomically or remain present but carry too little detectable flow. Angiographic non-perfusion alone cannot establish capillary disappearance. Reopening a surviving closed vessel could be clinically valuable, but rebuilding a lost vascular network is a different and more demanding claim. The intended target includes retina that has remained ischemic for months or years; that chronicity is a proposed scope, not an achievement established by the supplied studies.

significance.text: In diabetic retinopathy, capillary loss can cause tissue ischemia that promotes pathological neovascularization. These abnormal vessels can leak or bleed and contribute to severe retinal complications. A treatment that restored stable circulation and tissue oxygenation could reduce a hypoxic driver of proliferative disease. Its revolutionary contribution would be a restorative vascular capability beyond controlling complications or slowing further vascular loss.

The retained WHO fact sheet, dated 10 February 2026, attributes 3.9 million cases of distance vision impairment or blindness to diabetic retinopathy within the population whose vision impairment was preventable or remained unaddressed. This gives context for the disease burden. It does not estimate how many people have established retinal capillary dropout, retain salvageable retinal tissue, or would be eligible for a reperfusion treatment.

Conditional implications: if restored circulation remained functional and reduced ischemic signaling, it could lower neovascular complications and reduce the need for repeated treatment. Neither consequence follows automatically from seeing more vessels. Persistent disease could continue damaging the circulation, and neurons already lost to ischemia might not recover. Restored perfusion, visual recovery, and freedom from ongoing treatment therefore require separate demonstrations. Retinal vein occlusion remains a proposed application, but the supplied evidence supports it less directly than diabetic retinopathy.

missing_breakthrough.text: The missing capability is controlled restoration of a stable retinal microcirculation after established loss. The 2022 diabetic-retinopathy review identifies reperfusion as an unmet goal. The September 2025 ERG study addresses an earlier part of the disease process: reducing capillary regression in mice. Preserving vessels before they vanish does not establish the ability to reconstruct a depleted region after prolonged ischemia.

Engineering synthesis: a successful intervention would need to create or restore vessels in the correct retinal layers, connect them to an effective blood supply and drainage route, and produce flow through the tissue rather than isolated vessel structures or ineffective shortcuts. It would also need to establish barrier competence and vascular stability while avoiding uncontrolled neovascular growth. The central challenge is organized, functional vascular repair, not simply increasing vessel density.

Scientific synthesis: chronic disease introduces additional barriers. A reconstruction strategy must work in previously ischemic tissue, remain effective despite the underlying disease, and support whatever neural tissue remains viable. Experiments must also distinguish regeneration from preservation, reopening of existing vessels, and improved detection of previously slow flow. These distinctions determine whether an intervention has met the stated concept or demonstrated a narrower but potentially useful capability.

current_state.text: Wykoff and colleagues’ Eye review, dated 11 January 2022, reported that then-current anti-VEGF and steroid agents appeared unable to reperfuse areas of retinal non-perfusion in diabetic retinopathy, while regular retreatment might slow further accumulation of non-perfusion. This is a dated, cautiously expressed assessment, not evidence for a universal claim about every approved treatment in November 2026. The supplied review had access to the abstract; the article body was access restricted.

Ma and colleagues’ September 2025 PNAS study reported that endothelial Erg overexpression mitigated capillary regression in mouse oxygen-induced retinopathy and reduced early capillary regression in a murine diabetic-retinopathy model. The study distinguishes reduced regression from increased angiogenesis. In the oxygen-induced model, overexpression was induced before hyperoxic regression; in the diabetic experiment, it was induced before the measured regression endpoint. These results support capillary preservation under the tested conditions, rather than reconstruction of a long-standing human capillary-free region.

The ERG study’s human material consisted of postmortem expression comparisons, not a vascular regeneration intervention in living patients. The supplied evidence review assessed the main article through retained full-text XML, but did not inspect supplementary materials or figure images. Its findings therefore support the reported mouse experiments and their distinction between preservation and regeneration within that access scope.

The research attributes to Nanji and colleagues’ 2024 Acta Ophthalmologica meta-analysis a small slowing of non-perfusion progression with anti-VEGF and low-certainty evidence. No source artifact was retained for that paper, so the supplied review could not verify the effect, certainty assessment, or other details. This remains a research-reported finding requiring confirmation; the missing artifact is not evidence that the finding is false. Even if confirmed, slowing progression would address preservation rather than establish reconstruction after capillary loss.

The research also reports that human induced pluripotent stem cell–derived vascular cells improved mouse electroretinography in a diabetes model, identifying PMID 40940763 and a date of 30 August 2025. No retained source text or source URL was supplied for this report, so its date, experimental details, and outcome could not be assessed in the review. As described, a mouse electrical-response improvement would not by itself demonstrate integration into an established human capillary-free region or restoration of durable functional perfusion.

The supplied material does not establish the latest clinical or regulatory state as of 1 November 2026. Its dated evidence supports an unmet restorative goal and relevant mouse preservation results, while the search record supplied to the review was empty. It therefore cannot establish either that the full innovation has since been achieved or that no subsequent therapy has advanced beyond these findings.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: enroll eyes with well-characterized, established retinal non-perfusion, initially in a defined disease population such as diabetic retinopathy. Prespecify the duration and extent of non-perfusion and measure restoration within a defined area. If the claim is reconstruction after anatomical capillary loss, the protocol must provide evidence beyond absent angiographic flow to distinguish that loss from surviving closed or slow-flow vessels. A vein-occlusion cohort would require its own disease-specific justification and evaluation.
completion_criteria.label: Restoration measured within defined regions of established retinal non-perfusion

completion_criteria.text: Proposed vascular endpoints: show connected vessels carrying sustained flow through the treated region, evidence of improved tissue oxygenation, and barrier competence, including absence of pathological fluorescein leakage. Demonstrate that apparent reperfusion is not explained by imaging variability, improved detection of slow flow, or preservation of vessels that would otherwise have regressed. Slowing new dropout or preventing oxygen-induced regression in mice would be relevant supporting evidence, but would not complete the human reconstruction claim.
completion_criteria.label: Connected vessels sustain flow, improve oxygenation, and maintain competent barriers

completion_criteria.text: Proposed clinical and durability endpoints: prespecify meaningful reperfused area, follow-up duration, comparison treatment, rescue-treatment rules, and acceptable safety outcomes. Test whether reperfusion persists, neovascular complications fall, and injection requirements decline without sacrificing disease control. Visual function should be assessed separately because restored circulation may not reverse established neuronal loss. Reduced dependence on continuous anti-VEGF would strengthen the practical case, but should not be assumed from vascular imaging alone.
completion_criteria.label: Durable reperfusion reduces treatment burden while maintaining disease control

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and boundaries: confirm the result in independent studies and report performance across relevant levels of chronicity, disease severity, and remaining tissue viability. Identify where treatment fails, where ongoing vascular protection remains necessary, and whether benefit comes from reopening or reconstruction. These are proposed criteria rather than established consensus thresholds. Finite trials could establish benefit within tested populations and conditions, not universal repair of every ischemic retina.
completion_criteria.label: Independent studies reproduce benefits and define treatment limits

related_concepts.text: Early capillary preservation and suppression of pathological neovascularization overlap with OPH-08 through endothelial biology and ischemic retinal disease. The ERG mouse work illustrates preservation: it reduces regression before the relevant loss endpoint. Longer-acting anti-VEGF delivery instead changes how sustained treatment is supplied. Neither approach by itself demonstrates reconstruction after established capillary loss. Early preservation in retinopathy of prematurity is related, but the supplied evidence does not establish that it is easier than chronic reconstruction.

Roster comparison, based on the supplied concept titles: OPH-02, biological reconstruction of foveal cones, RPE, and their blood supply, has the closest overlap because both involve restoring vascular support. OPH-08 specifically targets established retinal capillary dropout; OPH-02 combines blood-supply reconstruction with replacement of specialized foveal tissue. OPH-07, programmable repair for photoreceptor and RPE gene defects, targets a different cellular and causal problem. OPH-11, prevention of progression from early or intermediate to late AMD, shares a retinal disease context but pursues prevention rather than reconstruction after established capillary loss.

Roster comparison, based on the supplied concept titles: OPH-01 concerns retinotopic reconnection of ganglion-cell axons to brain targets, and OPH-10 concerns arresting glaucomatous ganglion-cell death when pressure is not the therapeutic lever. These address neural connectivity or survival rather than retinal microcirculation. OPH-05 seeks patterned vision through the brain when the eye cannot transmit signals, while OPH-09 seeks reopening of the human visual critical period. Such neural capabilities could matter when vascular repair leaves residual visual impairment, but none is interchangeable with reperfusion.

Roster comparison, based on the supplied concept titles: OPH-03 reverses established cataract without lens removal, OPH-04 uses a manufactured cornea to clear vascularized stromal opacity, and OPH-06 controls axial eye growth. These concern lens transparency, corneal reconstruction, and ocular growth respectively. In particular, the vascularized corneal opacity in OPH-04 is a different tissue problem from restoring retinal capillaries that supply ischemic neural tissue. All remain distinct entries from OPH-08.

change_log.change: Preserved OPH-08 and its title while defining the target as durable functional circulation after established retinal capillary loss.
change_log.reason: The central restorative concept remains useful despite limitations in individual supporting assertions.

change_log.change: Separated angiographic non-perfusion, reopening of surviving vessels, and reconstruction after anatomical capillary disappearance.
change_log.reason: Absent detectable flow alone cannot prove that vessels have disappeared, and the distinction affects both mechanism and completion claims.

change_log.change: Replaced the universal present-day approval claim with the cautiously worded, dated 2022 assessment and paraphrased its reperfusion statement.
change_log.reason: The supplied evidence does not establish the November 2026 approval landscape, and the retained abstract differs from the candidate’s proposed exact quotation.

change_log.change: Expanded the ERG account to explain intervention timing, preservation versus angiogenesis, human postmortem material, and access limits.
change_log.reason: These details establish what the mouse results demonstrate and why they do not establish chronic human vascular reconstruction.

change_log.change: Retained the Nanji meta-analysis and iPSC vascular-cell reports with explicit verification limits.
change_log.reason: Their source text was unavailable to the supplied review; that warrants qualification rather than treating the reports as established or false.

change_log.change: Corrected the WHO source date to 10 February 2026 and clarified the denominator for the 3.9 million figure.
change_log.reason: The retained version supports a preventable or unaddressed vision-impairment burden, not an estimate of treatment eligibility.

change_log.change: Made reduced hypoxic signaling, fewer complications, visual recovery, and treatment independence separate conditional outcomes.
change_log.reason: Stable circulation does not guarantee elimination of persistent disease or recovery of neurons already lost.

change_log.change: Restricted leakage and bleeding claims to pathological neovascularization and qualified the vein-occlusion application.
change_log.reason: The evidence does not establish that all new vessels are abnormal and principally concerns diabetic retinopathy and retinopathy of prematurity.

change_log.change: Expanded proposed completion criteria to include chronicity, anatomical evidence, functional perfusion, durability, controls, rescue rules, reproducibility, and population boundaries.
change_log.reason: These distinguish restorative efficacy from preservation, imaging changes, and unsupported claims of universal benefit.

change_log.change: Removed the assertion that early prevention is easier and explained relationships to every other supplied roster entry.
change_log.reason: Comparative difficulty was not established, and related concepts should remain distinct rather than being merged.

unresolved_issues: The clinical and regulatory state as of 1 November 2026 remains unresolved because the supplied freshness search record is empty.
The Nanji meta-analysis result and low-certainty characterization require retained source text for verification.
PMID 40940763 lacks retained source text and a supplied URL; its date, cell intervention, functional result, and vascular integration remain unverified here.
The supplied evidence provides limited direct support for extending the concept to retinal vein occlusion.
A clinical protocol still needs a defensible method to distinguish anatomical capillary loss from closed or slow-flow vessels.
Meaningful reperfusion magnitude, chronicity, durability, safety limits, and rescue-treatment rules remain to be defined rather than treated as established standards.
Whether chronically ischemic retinal tissue retains enough viable neurons for visual recovery, and whether repaired vessels remain stable under continuing disease, remain open questions.

brief.title: Restoring blood flow where tiny eye vessels have vanished
possible: People whose diabetes has damaged the retina, the eye’s light-sensing tissue, could regain blood circulation in areas where tiny vessels have disappeared. A rebuilt network would carry oxygen through the tissue and keep blood from leaking into it.
why: When retinal tissue lacks oxygen, it can trigger abnormal vessel growth. Those vessels can leak or bleed. Restoring circulation could reduce this driver of severe diabetic eye disease and lessen the need for repeated injections.

sources.showed: WHO attributes 3.9 million cases of distance vision impairment or blindness to diabetic eye disease among people whose impairment was preventable or remained unaddressed.
sources.quote: Adults with vision impairment can experience lower rates of employment and higher rates of depression and anxiety.
sources.cited_for: Diabetic eye disease causes a substantial burden of vision loss.
sources.not_established: The figures do not identify how many people could benefit from rebuilding lost retinal vessels.

sources.showed: Their review linked retinal non-perfusion (RNP), areas without blood flow, to worsening diabetic retinopathy (DR), diabetes-related retinal damage. The medicines reviewed appeared unable to restore that flow.
sources.quote: overall, increasing RNP has been closely linked with worsening DR severity.
sources.cited_for: Restoring circulation addresses an unmet treatment goal in diabetic eye disease.
sources.not_established: The review does not demonstrate reconstruction of lost vessels or establish the performance of later treatments.

sources.showed: This is a combined analysis of studies of medicines that block a vessel-growth signal and their effects on worsening loss of retinal blood flow.
sources.cited_for: The analysis concerns slowing further loss of circulation.
sources.not_established: Slowing further loss does not establish that vanished vessels can be rebuilt.

sources.showed: Increasing ERG, a protein that controls gene activity in vessel-lining cells, reduced loss of tiny retinal vessels in mouse disease models. Early treatment also protected retinal nerve cells and vision in the oxygen-exposure model.
sources.quote: Erg  overexpression also reduces capillary regression in early stages of a murine DR model.
sources.cited_for: Early vessel loss can be reduced experimentally in mice.
sources.not_established: The experiments preserved vessels; they did not rebuild a long-depleted human retinal network.

shown: Ma and colleagues preserved capillaries, the smallest blood vessels, in mouse models of retinal disease by increasing ERG before the measured vessel loss. Their work demonstrates protection during early damage, rather than repair after vessels have long been absent.
missing: A treatment has yet to rebuild a connected vessel network in human retinal tissue after established capillary loss.
Rebuilt vessels must deliver oxygen, sustain blood flow and prevent harmful leakage or bleeding.
Lasting circulation must reduce abnormal vessel complications and injection needs while keeping disease controlled.

milestones.label: Restored circulation in clearly defined areas of established loss
milestones.explanation: A study would have to measure restored flow in defined areas with established loss of circulation and distinguish vanished vessels from closed survivors. This would establish what kind of repair occurred.

milestones.label: Connected vessels deliver oxygen without harmful leakage
milestones.explanation: Connected vessels would have to sustain flow, improve oxygen supply and prevent harmful leakage, beyond changes caused by imaging or vessel preservation. This would demonstrate functioning repair.

milestones.label: Lasting circulation reduces treatment needs while controlling disease
milestones.explanation: A comparative trial would have to show lasting circulation, fewer abnormal vessel complications and fewer injections without worse disease control, while assessing vision separately. This would establish practical benefit.

milestones.label: Independent studies reproduce benefits and identify treatment limits
milestones.explanation: Independent studies would have to reproduce benefits across differing disease severity, duration and surviving tissue, and distinguish reopening from rebuilding. This would define where treatment works and where protection remains necessary.

uncertain: A reliable way to distinguish vanished vessels from surviving vessels with closed or very slow flow remains to be defined.
It remains unclear how much nerve tissue survives prolonged oxygen shortage, or whether repaired vessels would withstand continuing disease.
The amount and duration of restored circulation needed for meaningful benefit, and acceptable safety limits, remain open questions.

page.title: Retinal revascularization after capillary loss
page.definition: New capillaries—the smallest blood vessels—restore blood flow through retinal tissue after anatomical capillary loss. The regenerated network maintains the blood–retina barrier, which limits leakage from blood into the retina.

goal.need: WHO’s fact sheet of 10 February 2026 attributes 3.9 million cases of distance vision impairment or blindness to diabetic retinopathy among people whose impairment was preventable or remained unaddressed. This does not estimate the population eligible for vascular regeneration. Retinal non-perfusion contributes to tissue hypoxia; restoring circulation after capillary loss addresses the vascular deficit.

statements.quote: BI 764524 uses a novel mode of action by inhibiting the Sema3A pathway to re-vascularize ischemic areas
statements.context: The developer describes the intended mechanism of its investigational treatment for diabetic macular ischemia. This passage states an objective, not demonstrated human regeneration.

statements.quote: We support research investigating the causes, mechanisms and treatments for retinal diseases, with the goal of preserving and restoring sight through retinal repair.
statements.context: This is a broader retinal-repair objective; it does not specify a capillary-regeneration endpoint.

completion.title: Regenerated capillaries sustain perfusion after documented anatomical capillary loss in human retina.
completion.criterion: A peer-reviewed, controlled human intervention study demonstrates new, connected capillaries carrying blood through retinal tissue with documented pre-treatment anatomical capillary loss, with persistent tissue perfusion and maintained blood–retina barrier function during follow-up. The evidence distinguishes new vessels from reopening or improved detection of pre-existing vessels. No numerical minimum for regenerated area, duration of prior loss or persistence is specified because no external reconstruction threshold was located.
completion.set_by: Atlas fallback; the cited bodies and protocols do not define completion of human retinal capillary reconstruction.
completion.basis: FDA retinal gene-therapy guidance, NEI research priorities, the 2026 diabetic-retinal-disease endpoints workshop, and HORNBILL and MAGIC protocols were searched for human reconstruction criteria. None supplied a completion threshold after anatomical capillary loss. This fallback directly tests the developer’s revascularization objective and distinguishes functional vessels from vascular structures alone.

milestones.title: A treatment increases retinal vessel regrowth between postnatal days 12 and 17 in mice.
milestones.criterion: In mouse oxygen-induced retinopathy, demonstrate greater normal vascular regrowth from postnatal day 12 (P12) to P17 than controls, accounting for initial vaso-obliteration, or vessel loss. Quantify pathological neovascularization separately; the convention sets no minimum percentage improvement. Lin et al. report endothelial-cell integration and revascularization in mice; their accessible abstract omits animal sample sizes. Ma et al. found no significant change in avascular or neovascular area after Erg induction at P12–P14, assessed at P17 (n=6 mice per group). These are neonatal models.
milestones.set_by: The angiogenesis-assay consensus authors, section 22 of their 2018 guidelines; this convention concerns the neonatal mouse oxygen-induced retinopathy model.
milestones.threshold_quote: the extent of vascular repair, which can be determined by examining the difference between VO at P12 and P17.

milestones.title: A retinal treatment reaches a human dose meeting HORNBILL’s <25% overdose-risk limit.
milestones.criterion: Reach a human intravitreal dose for which HORNBILL’s Bayesian model assigns <25% probability that the true ocular dose-limiting-event rate exceeds 25%, using events through day 8. The safety committee also reviews clinical data. HORNBILL tested 0.5 mg in 3 participants, 1.0 mg in 3 and 2.5 mg in 6; no single-dose limiting events occurred, and 2.5 mg advanced to repeated dosing. This is a dose-selection criterion, not proof of reperfusion.
milestones.set_by: Boehringer Ingelheim, HORNBILL registered protocol NCT04424290, version 6.0 of 7 October 2022, section 7.1; written for BI 764524 in diabetic macular ischemia.
milestones.threshold_quote: there should be less than 25% risk that the true ocular DLE rate is above 0.25.

milestones.title: A treatment improves retinal non-perfusion versus observation at 48 weeks with p < 0.05.
milestones.criterion: MAGIC (NCT05681884) compares faricimab 6 mg every 4 weeks with observation in adults with non-proliferative diabetic retinopathy and >5 disc areas of non-perfusion; target enrollment is 150. The test is a favorable between-group difference in baseline-to-week-48 non-perfused area on ultra-widefield fluorescein angiography, at p < 0.05. No minimum effect is specified; slower progression can satisfy this endpoint. Earlier HORNBILL data showed a week-22 foveal avascular-zone difference of −0.011 mm² (16 treated versus 7 sham eyes; one-sided p=0.23), without demonstrating anatomical regeneration.
milestones.set_by: MAGIC Study Group, published design of registered protocol NCT05681884; written for faricimab in non-proliferative diabetic retinopathy. This is a perfusion-progression endpoint, not a reconstruction criterion.
milestones.threshold_quote: Significance of all analyses will be determined at p < 0.05.

not_found: No peer-reviewed human intervention study demonstrating reconstruction after confirmed anatomical retinal capillary loss was located.
No published validation criterion distinguishing anatomical capillary loss from undetectably slow flow in a human reperfusion trial was located.
No MAGIC report of its 48-week primary outcome was located.
The full article and PDF for Lin et al. (2026) could not be opened; its abstract was accessible through the authors’ institutional publication record.
